1.q: Why does optics win over copper for long or fast links?

options.t: Fibre loss does not grow with frequency, copper loss does
options.why: Fibre loses about 0.2 dB/km at 1550 nm at any data rate; copper's loss rises with frequency, so beyond some distance or bandwidth optics pays for its conversion cost.

options.t: Photons are faster than electrons in a wire
options.why: Both signals travel at a good fraction of c; the difference is loss and bandwidth, not speed.

options.t: Optical circuits have compact transistors and memory
options.why: They do not: photonic circuits are linear and interferometric, with no compact equivalent of the transistor.

1.q: In decibels, how do you combine a link's laser power, losses and receiver sensitivity?

options.t: Subtract the losses from the launch power and compare with the sensitivity
options.why: A link budget in dB is a subtraction: launch power minus losses minus penalties, compared with the sensitivity, leaves the margin.
Averaging has no meaning here; powers and losses add and subtract in dB.
Multiplication is for linear ratios; in dB the same budget becomes additions and subtractions.

1.q: Which of these does silicon lack?

options.t: An efficient laser and the Pockels effect
options.why: Silicon's indirect gap gives no efficient laser and its symmetric crystal no Pockels effect; other materials fill these gaps.
Silicon's high index gives the strongest confinement of the common platforms.
That is silicon's main advantage.

2.q: What is the group index of a 500 × 220 nm silicon wire at 1550 nm, roughly?

options.why: That is the effective index; dispersion pushes the group index higher.
n_g = n − λ dn/dλ is about 4.2 for the wire, well above its effective index of about 2.4.
That is the material index; a guided mode's indices differ.

2.q: How far does the evanescent field reach into the oxide beyond a silicon core?

options.why: That is fibre-mode scale; the tail of a high-contrast silicon mode is much shorter.

options.t: Nothing reaches the oxide under total internal reflection
options.why: Total internal reflection still leaves an evanescent field on the low-index side.
The field decays as e^(−γx) with 1/γ of about 100 nm, which is why couplers, sensors and scattering depend on what is near the core.

2.q: A loss of α in 1/cm corresponds to how many dB/cm?

options.why: α_dB = 10 log₁₀(e) α = 4.343 α.
Decibels and natural-log units differ by a factor.
The factor is 10 log₁₀ e, not 10.

3.q: What sets a Gaussian beam's divergence?

options.t: Its waist: θ₀ = λ/(π n w₀)
options.why: Small waists diverge fast; that is why small chip modes need lenses or tapers to meet a fibre.
In linear optics the divergence does not depend on power.
A lens changes the beam, but the divergence of a given beam is set by its waist.

3.q: What is the mode-field diameter of standard single-mode fibre at 1550 nm?

options.why: SMF-28 has an MFD of about 10.4 µm at 1550 nm and 9.2 µm at 1310 nm.
That is the core of multimode fibre.
That is a lensed-fibre or inverse-taper spot.

3.q: A waist mismatch of a factor of two between two aligned Gaussian modes costs about:

options.why: Too large for a factor of two; that would take a far bigger mismatch.
Too small: the overlap of mismatched waists falls quickly.
η = (2w₁w₂/(w₁² + w₂²))² = 0.64, 1.9 dB.

4.q: Which platform offers everything, including gain, in one material?

options.why: Silicon has no efficient laser.
InP can guide, modulate, detect and amplify, at the price of higher loss and smaller wafers.
SiN has the lowest loss but no fast modulation, detection or gain.

4.q: Why does germanium detect C-band light?

options.why: Detection needs absorption, not the Pockels effect.
A detector must absorb.

options.t: Its direct gap of 0.80 eV puts its absorption edge near 1550 nm
options.why: λ_g = 1.24/E_g µm: 0.80 eV gives an edge at about 1.55 µm.

4.q: How do most modern silicon transceivers get their light?

options.why: Some use external lasers, but most integrate or attach III–V lasers.
Silicon does not lase efficiently.

options.t: From attached or bonded III–V lasers
options.why: Monolithic, hybrid, heterogeneous and transfer-printed integration bring III–V gain to silicon.

5.q: When is a symmetric slab waveguide single-mode?

options.why: The first higher mode appears at V = π; 220 nm of silicon in oxide is just below the 245 nm limit at 1550 nm.
2.405 is the single-mode limit of a step-index fibre.
Thicker films guide more modes.

5.q: What is the effective index of the TE0 mode of a 220 nm silicon slab in oxide at 1550 nm?

options.why: The slab solver gives 2.85, with n_g = 3.70 and 81 % of the power in the silicon.
That is bulk silicon; a mode's index lies between core and cladding.
That is the oxide cladding.

5.q: In thin silicon films, how do TM modes compare with TE modes?

options.why: It is the other way round in thin films.
TM's field jumps at the horizontal interfaces and spreads into the cladding, so its index and confinement are lower.
Only in a symmetric square guide could they be degenerate.

6.q: Which index sets a ring's free spectral range?

options.why: The FSR depends on how the phase changes with wavelength, which is the group index.
FSR = λ²/(n_g L): use n_g, about 4.18 for a 500 × 220 nm strip.
The cladding only enters through the mode.

6.q: A 1 nm thickness error shifts a silicon ring resonance by about:

options.why: That is the shift per nm of width.
About 1.4 nm per nm of thickness and 0.6 nm per nm of width.
Too small: thickness matters more than width.

6.q: When does a 500 × 220 nm-style silicon strip start to guide TE1 at 1550 nm?

options.why: Wider strips always guide more modes.
TE1 appears near 450 nm, so the standard 500 nm strip is close to the multimode limit.
That is far wider than needed.

7.q: What mostly causes the 1–3 dB/cm loss of silicon strips?

options.why: It grows with the index contrast and the field at the sidewall; wider strips and ribs lose less.
Undoped silicon is transparent at 1550 nm.
Straight strips lose this much too.

7.q: Why can silicon nitride carry watts at 1550 nm while silicon saturates?

options.t: SiN has a larger Kerr coefficient
options.why: Silicon's is larger; the problem is absorption.
Weaker confinement helps a little, but the key is the absence of TPA.

options.t: SiN has no two-photon absorption there
options.why: Silicon absorbs two photons together at 1550 nm and the free carriers this creates absorb more; SiN's wide gap avoids both.

7.q: What does periodic poling do in thin-film lithium niobate?

options.why: It is the lack of symmetry that gives χ⁽²⁾ in the first place.

options.t: Flips the nonlinearity every coherence length, so the second harmonic keeps growing
options.why: Quasi-phase-matching: with periods of about 4 µm in thin-film LN, the power grows at (2/π)² of the ideal.
Poling changes the sign of the nonlinear coefficient, not the loss.

8.q: Why does an Euler bend lose less than a circular one?

options.t: It ramps the curvature, avoiding the mode mismatch at the junctions
options.why: A circular bend's sudden curvature change makes a mismatch loss at each straight–bend junction.
It is usually longer; the gain is at the junctions.
The shape, not the material, makes the difference.

options.t: When it is made of oxide
options.why: Adiabaticity is about rate of change, not material.

options.t: Whenever it is longer than 1 µm
options.why: The required length depends on the modes involved.

options.t: When its width changes slowly compared with the local beat length to the nearest coupled mode
options.why: Then the mode follows the geometry without coupling power into other modes.

8.q: Roughly what bend radius suits a silicon TE strip?

options.why: Far too tight: the mode would radiate.
Silicon TE strips are fine above about 2–3 µm; TM, ribs and SiN need much more.
That is weakly confining SiN.

9.q: What is the cross-over length of two 500 × 220 nm strips 200 nm apart?

options.why: Ten times too short.
L_x = λ/(2Δn) = 37.8 µm at 200 nm gap, growing 2.4× per 100 nm of gap.
Ten times too long for this gap.

9.q: What does complete power transfer in a directional coupler require?

options.why: Any gap works if the length matches; small gaps only shorten it.
Identical guides are the usual choice.

options.t: Phase matching between the two guides
options.why: Without equal propagation constants, only part of the power crosses over.

9.q: Why is the cross-coupling term of a lossless coupler −j?

options.why: It holds for a lossless coupler.

options.t: Energy conservation requires the matrix to be unitary
options.why: A 90° phase between bar and cross outputs keeps the total power constant.

options.t: It is a convention with no physical meaning
options.why: It has consequences, for example in MZI interference.

10.q: Fed from one arm, a Y-branch combiner passes:

options.why: Half goes into an odd mode that radiates.
By symmetry, light from one arm excites even and odd modes equally; only the even one is guided out.
The even half still passes.

10.q: What is the beat length L_π of a 6 µm silicon MMI (TE)?

options.why: L_π ≈ 4n_r W_e²/(3λ) gives 90 µm; a 1 × 2 splitter is then 34 µm long.
Ten times too long.
Ten times too short.

10.q: A centred input to an MMI excites:

options.why: Overlap integrals vanish for the odd modes.
Symmetry forbids odd modes, which gives the short symmetric-interference images.
A symmetric input cannot excite antisymmetric modes.

11.q: The FSR of an unbalanced MZI with ΔL = 100 µm in a silicon strip at 1550 nm is about:

options.why: λ²/(n_g ΔL) with n_g ≈ 4.18 gives 5.75 nm.
Ten times too large.
Ten times too small.
Length sets the FSR, not the extinction.
Only through the couplers' wavelength dependence.
A 55/45 coupler caps the extinction near 26 dB.

11.q: How can an unbalanced MZI measure the group index on a chip?

options.why: Loss does not reveal the group index.
Measure the FSR, know ΔL, and solve for n_g.
Extinction tells about coupler balance, not n_g.

12.q: What is the FSR of a 10 µm-radius silicon ring at 1550 nm?

options.why: FSR = λ²/(n_g L) with L = 2π × 10 µm gives about 9.15 nm.
Ten times too small.
That is the Vernier FSR of two rings.

12.q: At critical coupling (t = a), the all-pass ring:

options.why: That is far from resonance.
Q_L = Q_i/2 at critical coupling; under-coupled rings have higher Q_L.

options.t: Has a full null on resonance
options.why: The coupled-in loss exactly matches the ring's round-trip loss, and the through port goes to zero.

12.q: Why can one through-port spectrum not tell under- from over-coupling?

options.why: They do; the ambiguity is in the fit.

options.t: The formula is symmetric in a and t
options.why: Swapping loss and coupling gives the same spectrum; use several gaps or an add-drop ring.
Even noiseless data has the ambiguity.

13.q: What period gives a first-order Bragg grating at 1550 nm in a 500 × 220 nm silicon strip?

options.why: Λ = λ/(2 n_eff) with n_eff = 2.446.
That would be second order.
Bragg reflection needs Λ = λ/(2n_eff).

13.q: A lossless Fabry–Pérot cavity with two 99 % mirrors, on resonance, transmits:

options.why: (1 − R)²/(1 − R)² = 1: equal lossless mirrors transmit everything on resonance.
Multiplying the two mirrors ignores the in-phase round trips.
That is one mirror; the round trips build up the light inside.

13.q: With loss inside, what does setting R₁ = R₂e^(−2αL) achieve?

options.why: The FSR depends on length and group index.
Loss still absorbs part of the light.
The front mirror leaks as fast as everything behind it loses; the rest is transmitted or absorbed.

14.q: What sets the DWDM channel grid?

options.t: The ITU frequency grid (for example 100 or 400 GHz spacing)
options.why: DWDM channels sit on the ITU grid; CWDM uses 20 nm spacing.
Linewidth must be far below the spacing, but it does not set it.
Unrelated to channel spacing.

14.q: Why does every ring demultiplexer need heaters and locking?

options.why: Heaters tune the wavelength, not the Q.
Heaters do not amplify.

options.t: Rings drift with temperature and fabrication
options.why: About 75 pm/K plus nanometres of fabrication offset: they must be tuned and kept on their channels.

14.q: In mode-division multiplexing, what does an asymmetric directional coupler phase-match?

options.why: Mode multiplexing works at the same wavelength.

options.t: TE0 of a narrow guide to TE1 of a wide bus
options.why: A 0.45 µm strip's TE0 matches TE1 of a 0.93 µm bus; the bus's own TE0 passes untouched.
That is a polarisation rotator.

15.q: Why are fibres tilted by 8–12° over grating couplers?

options.t: To avoid the strong second-order Bragg reflection of vertical coupling
options.why: At normal incidence the grating also reflects back into the waveguide.
Arrays can be made at any angle; the reason is optical.
Tilt does not mainly serve bandwidth.

15.q: A grating coupler's efficiency is the product of:

options.why: Those set phase matching, not efficiency directly.
They enter through directionality and overlap.
How much light goes up, times how well its profile matches the fibre mode.

15.q: What limits a grating coupler's 1 dB bandwidth to 30–40 nm?

options.why: Bandwidth is a property of the coupler.

options.t: The fibre's angular acceptance against the grating's angular dispersion
options.why: The beam angle changes with wavelength, and the fibre only accepts a narrow range of angles.
Silicon is transparent across the band.

16.q: Butt-coupling a 500 × 220 nm strip straight to SMF-28 loses about:

options.why: Far too optimistic: the modes differ greatly in size.
The mode must be expanded first, by an inverse taper or a spot-size converter.
Overlap losses are large, but not this large.

16.q: How does an inverse taper expand the mode?

options.why: A wider strip confines more, not less.
The taper alone does it; lenses are an extra option.

options.t: By narrowing the silicon tip so the mode spreads into the cladding
options.why: A 180 nm tip gives a 2.9 µm spot, 140 nm about 10 µm (TE).

16.q: What advantage does edge coupling have over grating coupling?

options.why: Small edge spots need tighter alignment.

options.t: Over 100 nm bandwidth and both polarisations
options.why: Grating couplers instead offer wafer-scale testing and relaxed alignment.
That is the grating coupler's advantage.

17.q: What is the 1 dB lateral tolerance of a lensed fibre on an inverse taper (2.5 µm spots)?

options.why: d = √(0.115 (w₁² + w₂²)): about ±0.6 µm, four times tighter than a grating coupler.
That is a pair of printed lenses with a 25 µm beam.
Far beyond any single-mode interface.

17.q: Facet-attached microlenses expand the beam to about 25 µm. What becomes harder?

options.why: A wide beam has a narrow far field: about ±1° of tilt for 1 dB.
Hundreds of micrometres of gap cost almost nothing.
It becomes ten times easier, about ±6 µm.

17.q: How is the alignment of a whole fibre array found quickly?

options.why: All fibres are the same.

options.t: Align a loopback between the outer fibres
options.why: When the loopback peaks, the rigid array is aligned for every channel.
The fibres are fixed in the array; aligning one pair aligns all.

18.q: How fast does a silicon ring drift with temperature?

options.why: dn_eff/dT ≈ 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ /K for a 500 × 220 nm strip gives about 75 pm/K.
A hundred times too much.
Silicon's thermo-optic coefficient is large.

18.q: Does P_π of a thermo-optic phase shifter depend on its length?

options.t: Yes: twice the length halves P_π
options.why: That is true of electro-optic V_π, not thermal P_π.

options.t: Yes: twice the length doubles P_π
options.why: Length cancels out.

options.t: No: longer heaters spread the same total power
options.why: P_π = λG'/(2 dn_eff/dT), with G' the thermal conductance per length.

18.q: What do trenches and undercuts trade?

options.why: Speed is the price.
Isolation lowers P_π (to 4.5 mW with an undercut) but slows the response (to 180 µs).
They concern thermal isolation, not optical loss.

19.q: In silicon, which carriers change the index more per unit of loss?

options.why: At 10¹⁸ cm⁻³, holes change the index three times more per unit loss than electrons.
It is the other way round.
They differ by about three.

19.q: What V_πL does a lateral PN junction at 5 × 10¹⁷ cm⁻³ give in a silicon rib?

options.why: Far beyond silicon's plasma effect.
Far worse than real devices.
With about 13 dB/cm of loss; doping trades efficiency against loss and capacitance.

19.q: What makes thin-film lithium niobate attractive for modulators?

options.why: LN does not provide gain here.

options.t: The Pockels effect: about 2.6 V·cm push–pull, low loss, > 100 GHz
options.why: A pure field effect, with no free-carrier loss and very fast.
That is a loss mechanism.

20.q: What is OMA in terms of average power and extinction ratio?

options.why: The optical modulation amplitude is the difference between the one and zero levels.
That overstates it.
That is not the modulation amplitude.

20.q: What does a ring modulator's Q trade?

options.why: Not a meaningful trade.

options.t: Nothing: higher Q is always better
options.why: Too high a Q limits speed.
High Q gives steep slopes and extinction but limits the photon-lifetime bandwidth.

20.q: PAM4 instead of NRZ at the same bit rate:

options.why: Smaller eyes cost decibels.

options.t: Halves the symbol rate, for a penalty of about 4.8 dB in eye amplitude
options.why: Each eye is a third of the swing; the penalty is the price of half the bandwidth.
It halves it.

21.q: What is the maximum responsivity at 1550 nm?

options.why: R = η λ[µm]/1.24 with η = 1.
Wrong units and value.
Without internal gain, at most 1.25 A/W.

21.q: What Q factor gives a BER of 10⁻¹²?

options.why: Far too low.
Far beyond what is needed.
BER = ½ erfc(Q/√2); Q = 3.49 gives the KP4 FEC threshold.

21.q: What dominates the noise of short-reach receivers?

options.why: Loss lowers signal; it is not a noise source.
Shot noise is small at these powers; the front end's thermal noise dominates.
Intensity detection ignores phase.

22.q: Why can a two-level system never invert?

options.t: Absorption and stimulated emission have equal coefficients, so pumping at most equalises the populations
options.why: B₁₂ = B₂₁; three- and four-level systems are needed.
The problem is the symmetry of B coefficients.
Not the reason.

22.q: Why does silicon emit light poorly?

options.why: Transparency at 1550 nm is unrelated to emission at its gap.
Not the reason.

options.t: Its band gap is indirect: B ≈ 10⁻¹⁴ against 10⁻¹⁰ cm³/s for InGaAsP
options.why: Radiative recombination needs a phonon, so it is very slow.

22.q: What does gain saturation look like?

options.why: Only for small signals.
Strong signals use up the inversion and the gain falls.

options.t: Gain grows without limit with intensity
options.why: It must saturate.

23.q: What is the condition for gain in a semiconductor?

options.why: The quasi-Fermi-level separation must exceed the photon energy (Bernard–Duraffourg).
Below the gap there is no interband transition.
Only above transparency.

23.q: What counts as the modal gain of a waveguide laser?

options.why: The mode only partly overlaps the gain.
Claddings have no gain.

options.t: Γg: the material gain times the mode's overlap with the active region
options.why: Only the part of the mode in the active layer sees gain.

23.q: What do quantum dots add over quantum wells?

options.why: Not their advantage.

options.t: Temperature stability and tolerance to defects
options.why: Which is why they suit growth on silicon.
Dots are III–V.

24.q: What is the threshold condition of a Fabry–Pérot laser?

options.why: Gain equals internal plus mirror loss; above threshold gain and carriers clamp.
That is transparency, not threshold.
Mirror loss must be paid too.

24.q: What threshold and slope does the 400 µm example laser have?

options.why: Off by ten in both.
Off by ten in both.
From the rate equations and the example's parameters.

24.q: How does a buried-heterostructure laser differ from a ridge laser?

options.t: Its ridge stops above the wells
options.why: That describes the ridge laser.

options.t: Its mesa is etched through the wells and buried again in regrown InP
options.why: No exposed surface, current only through the mesa, strong guiding.
It has wells, buried in InP.

25.q: How does a laser's relaxation frequency grow with current?

options.why: So bandwidth rises with bias until damping caps it.
It grows as a square root.
It grows with the photon density.

25.q: How does the α-factor change the linewidth?

options.why: It broadens.
It matters greatly.
Gain changes drag the index, adding phase noise.

25.q: Above about what feedback level can a laser become unstable?

options.why: Much weaker feedback is enough.
Coherence collapse can begin at −40 to −30 dB for typical lasers.
Far below the danger zone.

26.q: What side-mode suppression do single-frequency lasers typically need?

options.why: Enough that the other modes do not matter over fibre.
Far too little.
More than required.

26.q: How do λ/4-shifted DFB lasers tune?

options.why: That needs Vernier or external cavities.
Temperature tunes them a little.
They are the telecom workhorse but tune slowly and narrowly.

26.q: What Vernier FSR do 10 and 11 µm silicon rings give?

options.why: Far too small.
FSR₁FSR₂/|ΔFSR|, with a tuning gearing of 11.
That is one ring's FSR.

27.q: Why is self-heating worse for lasers on SOI?

options.t: The buried oxide insulates them thermally
options.why: Higher thermal impedance raises the temperature; thermal shunts help.
The issue is heat flow, not absorption.
They are electrically pumped like others.

27.q: In a heterogeneous laser, what moves the light from the III–V into the silicon?

options.why: The transfer is by supermode evolution.
That couples to fibre.

options.t: Widening the silicon along an adiabatic taper
options.why: The supermode follows from the MQW region into the silicon past the crossing near 0.85 µm.

27.q: Why can't a passive silicon circuit act as an isolator?

options.why: Size is irrelevant.

options.t: Lorentz reciprocity: linear, unbiased structures transmit equally both ways
options.why: Isolation needs a magnetic bias, time modulation or nonlinearity.
Loss does not break reciprocity.

28.q: What turns a laser chip into an SOA?

options.t: AR coatings and an angled waveguide that remove the feedback
options.why: Light passes once and is amplified, below the lasing threshold.
Current alone would make it lase.
The wells provide the gain.

28.q: What is the lowest possible noise figure of an amplifier?

options.why: Amplifiers always add noise.
Real SOAs can be better.
The quantum limit of a high-gain amplifier; input coupling loss adds to it.

28.q: How small must an SOA's facet reflections be?

options.why: They turn the SOA into a weak laser cavity.
Otherwise the gain ripples: 1.7 dB of ripple at 10⁻³ with 20 dB gain.
Far too reflective.

29.q: How should independent variations be combined in a design margin?

options.t: Not as stacked worst cases: use the spread
options.why: Stacking worst cases of independent variables is pessimistic; centre the design and use statistics.
That over-designs.
Margin must account for the spread.

29.q: What error does a Monte Carlo yield estimate carry?

options.why: Not the standard error.
Every finite sample has an error.
Binomial statistics: more samples, smaller error.

29.q: Which model should you use first?

options.why: Design needs models.

options.t: The cheapest that answers the question
options.why: Formulas and mode solvers first; one final 3D FDTD check.
Too slow for design sweeps.

options.t: Layers, validated cells, compact models, rules and the layer stack
options.why: Open PDKs make public designs possible.
Much more than that.
It is foundry data, not a simulator.

30.q: What does gdsfactory add to layout?

options.why: It is a design tool.
Testing is separate.

options.t: Layout as code, versioned and rerunnable
options.why: Designs can be swept, tested and regenerated.
Circuit simulation is routine.

options.t: From S-matrix compact models and a netlist
options.why: SAX and SiEPIC-Tools work this way.

options.t: Always with 3D FDTD of the whole chip
options.why: Far too expensive.
The time step must be short enough for the grid.
Too large a time step diverges.
3D has its own limit.

31.q: How does 3D FDTD cost grow as the grid is refined?

options.why: Far faster than linear.
Finer grids cost more.
More cells and smaller time steps.
It is very useful for tapers and MMIs.

options.t: Long devices, since length costs almost nothing
options.why: Each uniform section is exact; it struggles with radiation.
That is FDTD's strength.

32.q: What should you do before sweeping a design in any tool?

options.why: Check grid and settings; differences between tools are usually set-up differences.
Unconverged sweeps mislead.
Convergence is the first habit.

32.q: Which open tools cover mode solving and FDTD?

options.why: Open tools cover much of the work.
Not for field solvers.
With SAX for circuits and gdsfactory as glue.

32.q: Two tools built on the same method disagree. Most likely:

options.why: Check the set-up first.
Grids, materials, sources and monitors must match.
The method is the same.

options.t: 32-bit integers in database units, usually 1 nm
options.why: Hence a ±2.15 m range at 1 nm.
GDSII stores integers.
It is a vector format.

33.q: Why use hierarchy in a layout?

options.why: The mask is the same.
Flat layouts are legal, just large.

options.t: It keeps files small: 10 000 rings take 4 kB as an array, 37.7 MB flat
options.why: Cells are defined once and placed many times.

33.q: How does GDSII store a ring, which has a hole?

options.why: The cut line handles it.

options.t: As a polygon with a cut line
options.why: GDSII has no holes.
GDSII has no circles.

34.q: Which check catches a component moved 50 nm off its waveguide?

options.why: Every width and space rule can still pass.
Shapes may all be legal.
Connectivity checks catch it.

34.q: How should false DRC errors on curves be handled?

options.why: Real errors would then pass.
Count mistakes, not markers.

options.t: With tolerances, angle limits, on-grid drawing and written waivers
options.why: Never by blanket suppression.

34.q: In the chapter's test, how many real mistakes made the 373 markers?

options.why: There were real mistakes.
Most markers came from a few mistakes, an intended grating and a snapped coupler.
Markers are not mistakes.
Hydrogen implantation, bonding and splitting.
Not the standard process.
That leaves no film.

35.q: Why is tuning mandatory for silicon rings?

options.t: Rings have no resonances without heaters
options.why: They resonate; just at the wrong wavelength.
It shifts wavelength.

options.t: Wafer-scale variation spreads resonances by several nanometres
options.why: About 0.6 nm per nm of width and 1.4 nm per nm of thickness.

35.q: What does electron-beam lithography offer over DUV?

options.why: It resolves finer features.
DUV gives throughput and repeatability.
EBL is slow.

36.q: How are grating couplers de-embedded from a measurement?

options.t: With a loopback or a fitted envelope
options.why: Relative quantities are more robust than absolute losses.
Loopbacks remove them.
They dominate the raw spectrum.

36.q: What does testing edge couplers with a lensed fibre array demand?

options.why: Small spots need tight alignment.
Far beyond single-mode tolerances.

options.t: About ±0.6 µm on every channel at once
options.why: Printed lenses on chip and fibres widen that to about ±6 µm.

36.q: Why are grating couplers good for wafer-scale testing?

options.why: Edge couplers can lose less.

options.t: A fibre array can reach them anywhere on the wafer before dicing
options.why: Wafer maps reveal the process variation.
They are not.

37.q: What gives the propagation loss in a cutback measurement?

options.t: The slope of insertion loss against length
options.why: Its error bar shrinks with the spread of lengths.
The intercept is the coupler loss.
